title: Pass a rod through the tightest window you can
instruction: Pass the rod through the wall to the blue stand on the other side, using the smallest window you can, without touching the wall or dropping the rod.
context: In keyhole surgery, instruments and specimens go through ports and are taken by a second hand inside (surgical technologists and assistants, O*NET 29-2055.00 and 29-9093.00). Hand-to-hand transfer is a tested skill: peg transfer in the Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery manual skills test, where a dropped object is penalised. A smaller port means less trauma but less clearance. The instruction states the reward and the limits; the route, the grip and how much clearance to give up are left to the policy. The rod starts aimed at the strip of wall between the largest and the smallest window, so the start pose favours neither, and a straight push hits the wall. Neither gripper fits through a window, so the rod must change hands through the wall.
setup: Coordinates in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left). Wall: one 6 mm MDF panel, 26.5 cm long and 16 cm high, painted grey, standing upright and screwed to the table. Its centre is at (22.0, -8.5) and it is turned 45 degrees: near end at (12.6, -17.9), far end at (31.4, 0.9), one face toward the left arm. Three square windows are cut through it, all with their lower edge 4 cm above the table, with 2.5 cm of panel between neighbours and at both ends. From the near end: large 8 x 8 cm, small 3.5 x 3.5 cm, medium 5 x 5 cm. Rod: plain wood (pine or poplar), 26 x 2 x 2 cm, 50 g, with a pen mark round its middle, loose, lying flat on the table on the left arm's side with its centre at (8.2, 3.2). It lies square to the wall, in line with the strip of panel between the large and the small window, its far end 5 cm from the wall. Stand: a softwood block 14 x 8 x 3 cm, about 200 g, painted blue, screwed to the table on the right arm's side with its centre at (34.4, -18.8) and its long side parallel to the wall: 16 cm behind the wall, in line with the small window. Nothing else is on the table, and nothing is wired or taped to the wall or the rod.
scoring: Scored by eye, from a video of the trial that shows the windows and a top photo of the end. Score 0 if at any time the video shows the rod or any part of the robot (fingers, gripper, arm) touching the wall. Score 0 if at any time the rod is dropped: it leaves the grippers and falls more than 1.3 cm, onto the table or the stand. Putting the rod back does not undo either. Score 0 if at the end the mark at the rod's middle has not passed the wall, or if the rod's last pass was not through a window (over the top, round an end). Otherwise the window of the rod's last pass sets the value: large 0.4, medium 0.7, small 1.0. The score is that value if the rod lies at rest on the blue stand for 1 s with its middle mark over the block and both grippers at least 3 cm from it. It is 0.25 x that value if the rod is anywhere else behind the wall: still held, on the table, or still in the window. Doing nothing or refusing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.1, 0.175, 0.25, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0.
reset_notes: Put the rod back on its start mark. The wall and the stand do not move. The submitted runs use -E object_jitter=0.
fidelity: Wall, rod and stand are rigid boxes with one friction value (1.2). The wall is eight fixed boxes; the real panel is one piece. A touch is a proximity test: the rod's surface within 2 mm of the wall, or the robot's collision meshes within 5 mm, in place of judging contact by eye from the video. A drop is the rod's centre moving down faster than 0.5 m/s (a 1.3 cm free fall). Release is read from the measured arm joints. The rod's middle mark is not drawn in simulation.
